newsitem.title: UK: Euro Products - Markets look outside for direction.
newsitem.headline: Euro Products - Markets look outside for direction.

text.p: European oil products look set to move sideways this week but Nigerian fuel shortages could support the market and European holidays threaten to keep trading quiet, traders said.

Gasoline is showing some tightness in the ARA region which should help to support north European prices, while the Mediterranean will continue to be bolstered by Nigerian demand for 24 cargoes from now until early October.
Low octane material from the Black Sea is seen as particuarly attractive to the trader seeking to assuage Nigerian thirst and the Mediterranean is set to strengthen relative to NWE.
Naphtha looks set to remain flat for the first half of this week. Demand appears lacklustre in NWE and the Med and price moves will depend on whether Far Eastern demand kicks in.
Gas oil's outright price is seen ranging between $160 to $170 on front month IPE futures and a balanced physical market will keep differentials around last week's levels, traders said.
The start of the summer holiday season in some countries will help to slow physical market action, traders said.
Support for values last week came from talk of transport problems on railways leading to the Baltic port of Ventspils but these are likely to be resolved this week, traders said.

Heating oil barges are seen drifting along at 50 cents to $1 over July IPE, with low sulphur diesel at a premium of $5/$6. Low sulphur diesel cargoes will range around August IPE +$3.75. Regular 0.2 percent heating oil will range between $2 and $3 over August IPE, with gas oil moteur $1 dearer, they said.

High sulphur fuel oil has been little affected by crude's recent fall and traders said this was likely to continue. Cargoes would continue to draw support from tight supply with Russian exports getting absorbed.
"I see movement to the States and Mexico," one trader said. "I think you can find buyers for utility spec around $83 cif."
High sulphur barges were expected to continue to trade around last week's upside or the $85 mark, or a little higher if sellers continue to run away.
But some traders said that players wanting to price cargoes may bring the levels down to affect cargo quotes.
Low sulphur barges were seen steady to a bit weakish, with traders saying the little demand was sapping the market. Buyers were sidelined late last week to see where prices will settle.
But some said a boost could kick in if real buying interest comes in from Germany.
One percent may follow swaps that have moved a little southwards by the end of the week, with one trader saying this was "an indication of things to come".
